title: The Calendar Became My Reminder
cta: What date on the calendar is hardest for you?
fb:
Child estrangement turned my calendar into a list of things I'm not part of anymore.

I have four children, so the year is full of their dates. Four birthdays. The first day of school. Thanksgiving, Christmas, spring break. I keep track of all of them quietly.

Some of those days I can see coming for weeks. Others sneak up on me, an ordinary Tuesday that turns out to be a day I used to share with them.

I don't try to make those days normal anymore. I write them down, I plan one small thing, and I let them be hard without handing them the whole week.

What date on the calendar is hardest for you?

title: I Still Check My Phone
cta: Do you still check your phone?
fb:
When your estranged children aren't calling, you still check the phone. I do, anyway.

First thing in the morning. At red lights. Once more before bed. My kids are sixteen, fourteen, ten and seven. I know it isn't going to be them. I look anyway.

I used to be embarrassed by that. Now I think it's just what love does when it has nowhere to go. It's also why I've never changed my number.

If you do it too, you're not being foolish. You're being a parent.

Do you still check your phone?

title: What Is the Question You Are Afraid to Ask?
cta: What question have you been carrying alone?
fb:
A lot of estranged parent support starts with one question you've never said out loud.

Maybe it's "will my kids remember me?" Maybe it's "what are they being told?" Or the one that's hardest to admit: "is it wrong that some days I'm angry?"

Those questions get heavier the longer you carry them alone. Saying one, even without your name on it, tends to take some of the weight off.

You can ask yours on the site, anonymously. Nobody's going to tell you how to feel. Someone might tell you they've asked it too.

title: The Gift I Bought That Was Never Acknowledged
cta: Have you ever kept something you bought for your child?
fb:
Missing your children shows up in strange places. For me, one of them is the gift aisle.

When you can't reach your kids, every gift turns into a question. Will it get to them? Will they know who it's from? Will anyone tell me it arrived?

I've learned, slowly, not to send gifts as questions. If I send something, it's because I want my children to have it. Not because I need to hear back.

That's harder than it sounds. Some years I manage it.

Have you ever kept something you bought for your child?

title: How Do You Cope When You Miss Your Child?
keyword: how to cope with child estrangement
cta: What helps you get through the hardest days?
fb:
How do you cope with child estrangement on the days it flattens you? Honestly, there's no trick. There are a few things that help.

Keep your routine, especially on the dates you dread. Tell one person the truth about how you're doing, not the polite version. Get outside, even for ten minutes around the block. Write down what you'd say to your kids, and don't send it.

And lower the bar. On a bad day, making it to bedtime counts.

There are longer practical guides on the Resources page. None of them promise a fix. They were written for people standing exactly where you are.

What helps you get through the hardest days?

title: I Stopped Getting Progress Reports
cta: What ordinary part of parenting do you miss most?
fb:
Nobody warns you that being an estranged father means the school updates stop too.

Report cards. Picture day. The little things other parents complain about: a permission slip, a field trip form, a parent-teacher conference at a terrible time.

I have four kids in school, and I haven't had a recent school photo of any of them in years. I used to think that stuff was boring. I'd give a lot for one now.

It's not the big moments I miss most. It's the ordinary Tuesday ones.

title: Another Birthday Passed
cta: How do you handle your child's birthday?
fb:
Missing your child's birthday doesn't get easier. With four kids, I do it four times a year.

The date comes around. The memories come with it, and the phone stays quiet.

I don't pretend it's an ordinary day. I plan for it ahead of time, keep the day a little gentler than usual, and say the new age out loud, because it always surprises me.

It's a strange thing, marking the birthday of someone who isn't there. But they're still my children, and it's still their day.

How do you handle your child's birthday?

title: How to Write a Letter to an Estranged Child
keyword: how to write a letter to an estranged child
cta: Would a letter help you say what you cannot say aloud?
fb:
How to write a letter to an estranged child, from a dad who's thought about it a lot.

Keep it short. Say you love them. Tell them none of it was their fault. Don't ask why. Don't explain the adults' side or say anything about the other parent. Make it plain they don't owe you a reply.

Then read it back as if you were them, on a bad day. Cut anything that would put their guard up.

You're not trying to be understood. You're trying to leave the door open in a way that's easy to walk through.

There's a fuller guide on the Resources page.

title: The Part Nobody Sees
cta: What part of your story do people rarely see?
fb:
The pain of being an estranged father mostly happens where nobody's looking.

People see the version of me that shows up. At work, in line at the store, at a friend's cookout. That version's fine.

They don't see the drive home. The quiet house. The evenings I spend thinking about four kids growing up somewhere I can't see.

I'm not saying this for sympathy. I'm saying it because plenty of dads are carrying the same thing behind the same polite face, and hardly anyone asks.

What part of your story do people rarely see?

title: Can an Estranged Parent and Child Reconnect?
keyword: can estranged parent and child reconnect
cta: What would a healthy first conversation look like to you?
fb:
Can an estranged parent and child reconnect? Sometimes, yes. Nobody can promise you yours will, and I'd be wary of anyone who says they can.

My kids are still young. Sixteen, fourteen, ten and seven. A lot of what happens next isn't up to me, or even up to them yet.

What parents who've been through it tend to say: when it happens, it's usually slow, on the child's terms, and it starts small. A short message. A visit that ends early. Then maybe another one.

What you can do now is stay reachable, and keep becoming someone it would feel safe to come back to.

What would a healthy first conversation look like to you?

title: I Never Stopped Being Your Dad
cta: What does being a parent mean to you when contact is gone?
fb:
For an estranged father, contact can stop. Being a dad doesn't.

I still think like a parent. I still worry when the weather turns. I still see things in stores my kids might like and stop for a second.

For a while I didn't know what to call myself. A father with nobody to father. Now I think the answer's simpler. I'm still their dad. It just looks different from the outside.

That's not a claim on them. It's just the truth about me.

What does being a parent mean to you when contact is gone?

title: I Had to Learn to Stop Chasing the Outcome
cta: What are you learning to control, and what are you learning to release?
fb:
For years, everything I did about rebuilding a relationship with my estranged children was aimed at one result: getting them back.

Every message was a strategy. Every silence felt like a verdict. I judged each day by whether it had moved me any closer.

I had to learn to stop chasing the outcome. Not to stop hoping. Just to stop living as if my worth depended on it.

These days I try to do the right thing because it's right. Stay kind, stay reachable, never speak badly about their mom, look after myself. What happens next isn't mine to control.

What are you learning to control, and what are you learning to release?

title: How Do You Apologize Without Making It About You?
keyword: how to apologize to an estranged child
cta: Is there something you wish you had said differently?
fb:
How do you apologize to an estranged child without making it about you?

Name what you did, specifically. Say what it did to them, the way they'd describe it, not the way you'd prefer. Don't explain or defend. No "but." And never put them in the middle of what happened between the adults.

Don't turn the apology into a request for contact, either. A real one stands on its own, whether they reply or not.

It's one of the hardest things a parent can do. It's also one of the few things that's completely in our hands.

Is there something you wish you had said differently?

title: I Count the Years Differently Now
cta: Do you count the time too?
fb:
Family estrangement grief changes how you count time.

It's been more than five years. I count it in my kids' ages now. My oldest was a young boy. He's sixteen. My youngest was two. He's seven.

For a while that kind of counting felt like punishment. I'm trying to use it differently. Each of those years is also a year I kept going. A year I stayed kind. A year the door stayed open.

The time's passing either way. I'd rather it passed with me still here.

Do you count the time too?

title: The Empty Chair at the Table
keyword: missing your children during the holidays
cta: Who do you think about when you see an empty chair?
fb:
Missing your children during the holidays has a particular shape. Usually it's a chair.

Thanksgiving is this week. Everyone has a seat. The places my kids would sit stay empty. People are kind and don't mention it, and somehow that makes it louder.

Wherever I sit down to eat this year, I'm going to say one line before we start: I miss them, and they would always be welcome. Then I'll carry on.

If there's an empty chair at your table this season, there are a lot of us sitting near one.

Who do you think about when you see an empty chair?
